CHAPTER 15

## Eye, Ear, Nose, and Throat (EENT) Disorders

## CONTENT OVERVIEW

- Acute rhinosinusitis
- Allergic rhinitis
- Epistaxis
- Pharyngitis
- Epiglottis
- Infectious mononucleosis
- Eustachian tube disorder
- Tympanic membrane disorders
- Hearing loss
- Red eye evaluation
- Glaucoma
- Retinopathy
- Eye pain

## NOTES

## SINUS, NOSE, AND OROPHARYNX COMPLAINTS

## Acute Rhinosinusitis Overview

- Symptomatic inflammation of the paranasal sinuses
- Etiology
- $ Viruses (most common)
- $ Bacteria (less than 2% of cases)
- $ Fungal (rare)
- $ Allergies
- $ Irritants
- $ Dry air
- $ GERD

## Paranasal Sinuses

Joshua Lanclos/APEA

<!-- image -->

© Kateryna Kon/Shutterstock

<!-- image -->

## Acute Rhinosinusitis (ARS)

## Symptoms

- Nasal congestion
- Purulent nasal discharge
- Facial pain/pressure (worse with bending down)
- Maxillary dental pain
- Fatigue, fever, cough, etc.

## Physical exam

- Sinus tenderness
- Mucosal erythema
- Purulent posterior pharyngeal/nasal secretions
- Air-fluid levels on transillumination

## ACUTE VIRAL RHINOSINUSITIS

- Viral etiology: rhinovirus, parainfluenza, RSV, etc.
- Expected course
- $ Symptoms peak days 3-6 days
- $ Resolves in 10-14 days
- $ ARS: <4 weeks
- $ Chronic rhinosinusitis: >12 weeks

| Medication                   | Symptom Relief                                                                  |
|------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Saline irrigation            | Recommend for symptomatic relief                                                |
| Intranasal glucocorticoids   | Recommend for symptomatic relief                                                |
| Mucolytics                   | Guaifenesin thins secretions to promote mucous drainage.                        |
| Topical & oral decongestants | May help nasal congestion                                                       |
| Antihistamines               | Not recommended; may cause over drying of mucosa. Consider if allergic rhinitis |

## QUESTION #1

Which of the following presentations are most consistent with acute bacterial rhinosinusitis?

1. Symptoms are most severe on days 3-6.
2. OTC medications do not provide complete relief.
3. Symptoms are improving, then suddenly become severe again.
4. Nasal discharge is green and blood tinged.

## Acute Bacterial Rhinosinusitis (ABRS)

- Secondary bacterial infection of the sinuses
- $ Persistent symptoms: ≥10 days without improvement
- $ Severe symptoms: at onset and lasting at least 3 days
- Fever, purulent nasal discharge, ill-appearance
- $ Worsening symptoms: symptoms improve, then worsen again ("double-sickening")

## Bacterial Sinusitis

## Pathogens

- Streptococcus pneumoniae
- Risk for complications: orbital cellulitis, meningitis
- Haemophilus influenzae
- Moraxella catarrhalis

## Management

- Amoxicillin/amoxicillin/clavulanate × 5-7 days
- Recent antibiotic exposure:
- High-dose amoxicillin/clavulanate ER (2000/125 mg BID)
- Penicillin allergy:
- Doxycycline
- Third-generation cephalosporin

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES

## QUESTION #2

A patient reports sneezing, postnasal drip, and nasal congestion. Considering the most likely diagnosis, what other findings are expected?

1. Purulent nasal discharge
2. Boggy, gray nasal turbinates
3. Petechiae of the posterior pharynx
4. Tenderness to the sinuses on palpation

## Allergic Rhinitis

Inflammation of the mucous membranes of the nasal tract

- Symptoms
- $ Sneezing
- $ Rhinorrhea
- $ Postnasal drip
- $ Nasal congestion
- $ Nasal/mucosal itching
- $ Infraorbital edema (allergic shiners)
- $ Allergic conjunctivitis

## Allergic Rhinitis Management

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

© Refluo/Shutterstock

## Intranasal glucocorticoids (fluticasone, mometasone, beclomethasone)

- Preferred monotherapy for persistent symptoms (nasal & conjunctival)

## Intranasal antihistamines (azelastine, olopatadine)

- Intranasal administration is superior to oral antihistamines.

## Second-generation oral antihistamines (fexofenadine, loratadine, cetirizine)

- Less sedating than first generation

## Intranasal decongestants (oxymetazoline)

- Beneficial with severe congestion administered prior to INCS or INAH

Systemic corticosteroids: very severe or intractable symptoms

Oral decongestants and leukotriene receptor antagonists: Risks may outweigh benefits

## QUESTION #3

A 14-year-old with a history of allergic rhinitis and asthma is started on montelukast. The NP should advise the caregiver to monitor for serious side effects including:

1. suicidal thoughts.
2. somnolence.
3. headache.
4. anuria.

## Decongestant Adverse Effects

Pseudoephedrine/Phenylephrine (systemic)

Contraindications

- Uncontrolled hypertension
- MAOI therapy (last 14 days)

## Caution:

- Closed-angle glaucoma
- CAD
- Hyperthyroidism
- Urinary retention
- Potential for pseudoephedrine misuse
- $ Athletes use as a stimulant
- $ Illegal production of methamphetamines

Oxymetazoline (local)

- Overuse ➔ Rhinitis medicamentosa

## Epistaxis

- Anterior (90%)
- $ Kiesselbach plexus: anastomosis of five major arteries, very vascular
- Posterior bleeds (5-10%)
- $ Older patients
- $ Difficult to control
- ER referral

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Epistaxis Characteristics

- Bimodal: children and older adults
- Etiology
- $ Idiopathic (most common)
- $ Epistaxis digitorum (nose picking) / trauma
- $ Foreign body (children, dementia)
- $ Alcohol, cocaine use
- $ Infection/allergies
- $ Bleeding disorder*
- $ Anticoagulation*
- $ High blood pressure*
* Higher risk for posterior/severe nosebleed

## Epistaxis Management

Refer if hemodynamic stability, severe (duration >30 min or over a 24-hour period) Nasal compression:

- Pinch nose tightly for ≥5 minutes.

Nasal packing

Topical decongestant

- Oxymetazoline

## Cautery

- Visualization of bleeding
- Silver nitrate stick

## Pharyngitis/Tonsillitis

Viral: 50-80% of cases

- Usually: "common cold" viruses
- Less common: HIV, cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein-Barr virus

Bacterial: less common

- Group A Streptococcus (GAS)
- Other respiratory bacteria

Noninfectious

- GERD
- Dry air
- Smoke

<!-- image -->

© ollo/iStock/Getty Images Plus/Getty Images

<!-- image -->

© rob9000/Shutterstock

<!-- image -->

## Streptococcal Pharyngitis

- 5-15% adults Group A Streptococcus
- Symptoms: FLEA:
- $ Fever
- $ Lack of cough
- $ Exudate
- $ Anterior cervical adenopathy
- Potential for serious complications

## Centor Criteria (Modified): Streptococcal Pharyngitis

Four-point scoring system that guides testing and empiric treatment of streptococcal infections

## SCORE 0, 1, 2

- Low risk
- Testing not recommended

## SCORE 3

- Moderate risk
- Consider testing

## SCORE 4-5

- High risk
- Recommend empiric antibiotics, consider RADT or culture

## QUESTION #4

Which patients with pharyngitis should receive a rapid strep test?

| Patient                                                                                                        |   Centor Score | Swab?   |
|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------|---------|
| A 13-year-old with fever, enlarged posterior cervical lymph nodes, and tonsillar exudate                       |              3 |         |
| A 60-year-old daycare worker with tonsillar exudate, temp 101.2 ° F, and swollen anterior cervical lymph nodes |              2 |         |
| A 25-year-old with cough and temperature of 99.4°F                                                             |              0 |         |

|----------------------------------|----------|
| Absence of cough                 |        1 |
| Enlarged anterior cervical nodes |        1 |
| Temperature over 38°C (100.4°F)  |        1 |
| Tonsillar exudates or swelling   |        1 |
| Age 3-14                         |        1 |

| Age 45 years or older            |       -1 |
| Cumulative score                 |          |

## NOTES

## NOTES GAS Pharyngitis Testing

Rapid antigen detection test (RADT) kits

- 70-90% sensitivity
- 90-100% specificity

## THROAT CULTURE

- 90-95% sensitivity
- 95-99% specificity

Tests are only as good as your sample!

## Strep Pharyngitis Treatment

## First line: penicillin

- Pen G, Pen V, or amoxicillin

## Alternatives (if PCN allergic)

- Type IV hypersensitivity: 1st gen cephalosporins
- Type I hypersensitivity: 2nd or 3rd gen cephalosporins (cautious use)
- Clindamycin
- Clarithromycin ➔
- Azithromycin

Check GAS community

resistance rates

Duration: 10 days except azithromycin (5 days)

## QUESTION #5

A patient has been diagnosed with pharyngitis and the NP suspects infection with Group A Streptococcus. What complications are not associated with Group A streptococcal oropharyngeal infections?

1. Periorbital cellulitis
2. Rheumatic fever
3. Acute glomerulonephritis
4. Peritonsillar abscess

## QUESTION #6

A patient arrives to the clinic reporting a severe sore throat. The patient is observed sitting in a tripod position, mouth breathing, and has a muffled voice. Because on these findings, the NP suspects:

1. viral pharyngitis.
2. bacterial tonsillitis.
3. epiglottitis.
4. peritonsillar abscess.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Epiglottitis

- Inflammation and edema of the epiglottis
- Caused by Haemophilus influenzae type B (HiB)
- $ Other: S. pneumoniae, S. aureus, others
- ER Referral! Rapidly progressive airway obstruction
- Warning signs:
- $ Tripod position
- $ Mouth breathing
- $ Drooling
- $ Dysphagia
- $ Muffled voice ("hot potato")
- $ Neck radiograph-"thumb sign"

<!-- image -->

© medicalstocks/Shutterstock

## QUESTION #7

A college student who has been feeling ill for 3 days tests positive for infectious mononucleosis. What symptoms is this patient likely to report?

1. Anorexia
2. Sore throat
3. Vomiting
4. Enlarged anterior cervical lymph nodes

## Infectious Mononucleosis

- Classic symptom tetrad
- $ Fever
- $ Pharyngitis
- $ Fatigue
- $ Lymphadenopathy (posterior)
- Splenomegaly (50%)

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

© Designua/Shutterstock

## NOTES

## NOTES Mononucleosis Diagnosis

## DIAGNOSIS CAN BE MADE ON CLINICAL PRESENTATION.

Viral capsid antigen (VCA): EBV specific antibodies

|                              | Anti-VCA IgM   | Anti-VCA IgG                   | EBV Nuclear Antigen                   |
|------------------------------|----------------|--------------------------------|---------------------------------------|
| Present in serum             | Onset-6 wk     | Acute phase, positive for life | 2-4 mo after onset; positive for life |
| Acute                        | Pos            | Pos                            | Neg                                   |
| Acute or past                | Neg            | Pos                            | Pos                                   |
| Past                         | Neg            | Pos                            | Pos                                   |
| Late primary or reactivation | Pos            | Pos                            | Pos                                   |

Monospot: possibility of false-negatives

## QUESTION #8

A patient presents with intermittent pain in the left jaw and cheek for the past week. What diagnoses should be included in the differential? (Select all that apply.)

1. Trigeminal neuralgia
2. Temporomandibular joint (TMJ) dysfunction
3. Acute rhinosinusitis
4. Dental infection

<!-- image -->

TIP: Consider dental etiology when patient is present with facial/jaw pain.

## EAR COMPLAINTS & HEARING LOSS

## QUESTION #9

What is the primary function of the eustachian tube in the middle ear?

1. Transmitting vibrations to the inner ear
2. Equalizing air pressure
3. Protecting the inner ear from loud noises
4. Producing earwax to trap dust and debris

<!-- image -->

## Eustachian Tube Dysfunction

Equalizes air pressure between atmosphere and middle ear

## Obstructive symptoms

- Ear pain
- Muffled hearing
- Tinnitus; ear popping
- Imbalance

## Complications

- OM with effusion
- Retracted ear drum
- Chronic otitis media

## Treatment

- Treat the underlying cause.
- Allergic rhinitis, rhinosinusitis, reflux, etc.

## Tympanic Membrane Conditions

## NOTES Hearing Screening

- United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) does not recommend universal screening in adults.
- Whisper test is useful for screening if the patient is not aware of hearing loss.
- Audiometry referral for any complaint of hearing loss
- $ Determines
- Type:
- $ Conductive
- $ Sensorineural
- $ Mixed
- Severity

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #10

What is the most important reason to optimize hearing in an older adult?

1. Hearing loss will impact employment opportunities if not corrected.
2. Hearing loss reduces ability to perform daily tasks independently.
3. Older adults who cannot hear are not legally able to drive.
4. Hearing loss can lead to understimulation, isolation, and potential cognitive decline.

## Conductive Hearing Loss

Problem with outer/middle ear (i.e., cerumen buildup, FB, etc.)

- Sound cannot transmit through canal/TM.
- Often caused by obstruction
- $ Cerumen impaction
- $ Foreign body (including headphones)
- $ Otitis externa
- $ Otitis media with effusion
- $ Eustachian tube dysfunction
- Chronic causes are less common.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## Sensorineural Hearing Loss

- Due to pathology of cochlea, CNVIII, or CNS
- Presbycusis is the most common cause.
- $ Age-related hearing loss due to genetic factors and noise exposure
- $ Difficulty hearing mid-high frequency sounds, speech distortion, tinnitus (crickets, ringing, bells)
- Other causes
- $ Acoustic lesions, trauma, ototoxic medications, acute/chronic noise exposure, hereditary disorders, Ménière's disease

Joshua Lanclos/APEA

## QUESTION #11

Which of the following is true of Ménière's disease?

1. Dizziness is worse with head movement.
2. Disease course is persistent and predictable.
3. Dix-Hallpike confirms the diagnosis.
4. Hearing loss may become permanent.

## Auditory Emergency

Refer to ENT or ER for:

Hearing loss that is:

- Abrupt onset
- Unexplained
- Unilateral
- Sensorineural hearing loss

## Hearing Loss: In Office Testing

Weber Test

- Conductive loss: louder in affected ear
- Sensorineural loss: louder in unaffected ear

## Rinne Test

- Normal: air louder than bone conduction
- Abnormal: bone louder than air conduction

## Unilateral Hearing Loss Algorithm

## NOTES

## NOTES Name the Diagnosis

Presents with tragal tenderness and a narrow, inflamed ear canal

Presents with severe ear pain, otorrhea, hearing loss, and tenderness of the mastoid process

Presents with ear pain, mild hearing loss, and bulging of the tympanic membrane; may report a recent upper respiratory infection (URI)

## EYE COMPLAINTS

## QUESTION #12

An adult patient presents with painless swelling of the upper eye lid for the past 4 weeks. There is no conjunctival drainage or injection. Which of the following diagnoses is most consistent with this presentation?

1. Chalazion
2. Hordeolum
3. Pterygium
4. Pinguecula

## Red Eye Evaluation

Major causes

- Uveitis, iritis: inflammation
- $ Infections, autoimmune, trauma
- Acute angle-closure glaucoma
- $ Rapid increase in intraocular pressure
- Keratitis: corneal inflammation
- $ Infections, injuries, contact lens
- Trauma

## Minor causes

- Conjunctivitis
- Blepharitis
- Minor foreign body

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

© Andrei310/iStock /Getty Images Plus/Getty Images

<!-- image -->

## Red Eye Evaluation

| History                                                | To Ophthalmology   |
|--------------------------------------------------------|--------------------|
| Change in vision                                       |                    |
| Foreign body sensation with inability to keep eye open |                    |
| Photophobia                                            |                    |
| Foreign body sensation, scratchy, gritty               |                    |

<!-- image -->

## Which Presentation Needs Referral to Ophthalmology?

| Patient Presentation                                                                      | Referral?   | Diagnosis?   |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------|--------------|
| Bilateral mucoid discharge, nasal congestion, sneezing                                    | No          |              |
| Sudden severe pain, redness, and blurred vision of right eye                              | Yes         |              |
| Presence of flashers, floaters, then a "curtain" of vision loss on the periphery          | Yes         |              |
| Painless, bright red pool of blood on the surface of the eye that appeared after coughing | No          |              |

## Angle-Closure Glaucoma

Closure of anterior chamber angle leads to increased IOP and optic neuropathy

## TYPES OF GLAUCOMA

<!-- image -->

© Timonina/Shutterstock

- MEDICAL EMERGENCY
- Sudden severe eye pain
- Headache
- Nausea, vomiting
- Blurred vision
- Halos around lights
- Most common
- Gradual development
- Asymptomatic early stages
- Vision loss due to optic nerve damage
- Blindness, if not treated early

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Age-Related Macular Degeneration

- Dry: gradual vision loss
- Wet: rapid and severe vision loss
- Symptoms
- $ Central blind spot (scotoma)
- $ Curving of straight lines
- $ Normal peripheral and color vision

Leading cause of permanent vision loss in older adults

## Retinopathy

- Retinal damage caused by:
- $ HTN
- $ DM
- $ Macular degeneration
- $ Genetic factors
- Signs
- $ Cotton wool spots
- $ Flame hemorrhages
- $ Hard exudates
- $ Arteriovenous nicking

## Eye Pain

Refer emergently to the ER or Ophthalmology unless noted

| Condition        | Etiology                                           | Symptoms                                                                                                              |
|------------------|----------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Hyphema          | Typically posttraumatic, blood in anterior chamber | · Grossly apparent blood at base of iris (possible) · Decreased visual acuity                                         |
| Corneal abrasion | Posttraumatic, contact lens wear                   | · Fb sensation · Unable to keep eye open · Defect visible with fluorescein staining · Specialty referral if indicated |

<!-- image -->

© ttsz/iStock /Getty Images Plus//Getty Images

<!-- image -->

## Eye Pain

Refer emergently to the ER or Ophthalmology unless noted

| Condition   | Etiology                                                                          | Symptoms                                                                                                                 |
|-------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Iritis      | Posttraumatic; autoimmune conditions like Crohn disease; infectious causes        | Hallmark symptom: pain in affected eye when light stimulus shined in unaffected eye; blurred vision, may include redness |
| Scleritis   | Underlying rheumatologic or autoimmune disorders                                  | Diffusely injected, redder than that of conjunctivitis, headache, severe pain                                            |
| Keratitis   | Herpes virus, bacterial (Staphylococcus, Pseudomonas) overnight contact lens wear | Watery discharge, blurred vision ciliary flush; dendritic lesions (herpes) on slit lamp exam/ fluorescein staining       |

## EXAM CHECKLIST

- Acute sinusitis
- Epistaxis
- Hearing assessment
- Pharyngitis/epiglottitis
- Mononucleosis
- Otitis media/externa
- Periorbital cellulitis
- Conjunctivitis, blepharitis
- Retinopathy
- Macular degeneration
- Eye pain emergencies
- Know clinical presentation (subjective, objective findings)
- Know how to diagnose
- What is in differential diagnoses?
- Pharmacologic, nonpharmacologic management
- Follow-up care
- Recognize normal course
- When to refer
